newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Peters anoints arch-enemy in NZ coalition.
newsitem.headline: Peters anoints arch-enemy in NZ coalition.

text.p: The kingmaker of New Zealand politics bestowed the crown on his former arch-enemy on Tuesday.

Winston Peters, by choosing the conservative National Party as his coalition partner, ended two months of political suspense during which he commanded centre stage and revelled in holding the balance of power.
Peters, a rebel who formed the New Zealand First Party in 1993 after quitting the governing National Party, will be deputy prime minister and treasurer in the new government.
Opponents and political analysts said Peters faced a tough job selling the coalition deal to his supporters, including large numbers of Maoris traditionally hostile to National.
"I think Winston Peters is dog meat," said Richard Prebble, leader of radical free-market Act New Zealand.

Once dubbed "Luigi" for his dark good looks and stylish double-breasted suits, Peters is a charismatic, populist leader who learned his trade from the fiery Sir Robert Muldoon, prime minister from 1975 to 1984. Muldoon once tipped Peters to be New Zealand's first Maori prime minister.
No other New Zealand politician inspires such hero-worship in his supporters. None draws such condemnation and vitriol from his detractors.

As Peters negotiated for nearly two months with both National and Labour, some media commentators accused him of holding the country to ransom despite winning just 13 percent of the vote in October's general election.
The blanket secrecy surrounding the talks, critics said, was the very opposite of the open, accountable style which Peters publicly espoused.

But Peters, a lawyer of half-Maori, half-Scottish descent, refused to be hurried. No stranger to controversy, he once missed a session of coalition talks after being involved in a 2 a.m. altercation with patrons of a Wellington restaurant.
Exposing scandals is Peters' stock in trade, and his probing forced the government in 1994 to launch an inquiry into use of the Cook Islands as a tax haven by major New Zealand companies.

Sometimes his allegations have backfired. Earlier this year a judge ordered to him to pay a total of NZ$125,000 (US$88,000) in defamation damages and costs to a prominent businessman who, Peters claimed, had attempted to bribe him.
New Zealand First -- opponents dub it "Winston First" -- fought the election on promises to put ordinary people's welfare above the interests of foreigners and big business.
"We think the resources of this country should be owned by the people of this country for the employment and wealth-creation and the benefit of this country," Peters said.
His support rose to a peak of 30 percent last February after Peters promised to cut immigration "to the bone", but he rejected accusations of racism towards Asians.
